title: The hunter's accidental fast
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: a hungry hunter waits all night in a bilva tree, and his fast turns into worship
carry: upavasa: the fast is staying near shiva
tomorrow: The hunter in the bilva tree

cards: A hunter goes into the forest on Shivaratri, though he has no idea it's Shivaratri. He hasn't eaten all day, and he's caught nothing.
At dusk he climbs a bilva tree beside a pool, with a pot of water, to wait for animals coming to drink. He doesn't know there's a Shiva linga in the roots below him.
Each time he shifts on the branch, a little water spills, and a few bilva leaves drift down onto the stone.

teach.h: A HUNTER IN A BILVA TREE.
teach.b: He didn't choose to fast. He simply has nothing.

But in the Shiva Purana's telling, that hungry night still counts: a fast, a night awake, water and bilva on the linga, all kept without knowing, and Shiva takes notice. The next days follow him through the night.
Today, look at the empty stomach. Here's the teaching. The Sanskrit word for a fast is upavasa.
Many teachers hear in it upa, near, and vasa, dwelling: staying near. A Hindu fast isn't mainly about going without. It's keeping close to the one the day is for.
The hunter went hungry by accident, and his hunger kept him alert in a tree above a linga he couldn't even see.
Families who fast on purpose turn that same hunger toward Shiva: each pang is a small reminder of whose day it is. And the fast sits inside a vow, not a punishment.

teach.h: NOT TOO MUCH, NOT NONE AT ALL.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all.
So families make room for children, the sick, and anyone a fast would hurt, and many keep a lighter vow of fruit and milk; a vow kept honestly is still the vow.
Look back at the week: one bow for everyone, Ganga in Shiva's hair, a boy asking for milk, the poison and the bath, the endless pillar, Parvati's vow, and now a hungry hunter.
Each time, something hard brings someone nearer to Shiva.

how: Hindus who fast on Maha Shivaratri keep different vows: some take only water, some take fruit, milk and special fasting foods such as sago, and the fast is usually broken the next morning after worship.

games.q: it's midnight on Shivaratri and you're hungry. what does upavasa ask you to do with the pang?
o: let it turn you back toward the one you're staying near.
scroll until you forget about food.
games.why: upavasa, staying near. the hunter's hunger kept him alert above a hidden linga; on purpose, each pang turns you back toward Shiva.

practice: Sooner or later something will tug at you, an itch, a thought of food, the urge to check a message; don't act on it or fight it, just ask quietly, who am I staying near, and come back. Each tug is one more return.
If you pray, let each return carry om namah shivaya, or the name of God you use; if you don't, let the breath be the place you stay near.
